title: Genesis 46. The Cup of Descent.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 46. The Cup of Descent.
Israel traveled with all that he had, and came to Beersheba,
and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
Israel.
The text uses the covenant name.
The man who said enough,
I will go and see him before I die, now moves.
The Cup of hope produces action.
The father who said if I am bereaved,
I am bereaved now travels with everything he has toward the son he thought was dead.
Beersheba.
The southern boundary of Canaan.
The last stop before leaving the land.
Abraham sojourned at Beersheba.
Isaac built an altar there.
Jacob now sacrifices at the same place his father worshiped.
Three generations, same place, same God.
The covenant's geography, Beersheba is where the land meets the wilderness.
The last altar before the border.
Jacob offers sacrifices before crossing the boundary.
Not impulsive movement, worship first.
The man who said I will go goes to God before going to Egypt.
The Jacob who fled from Esau without stopping to listen now stops.
The Jacob who wrestled and demanded a blessing now sacrifices.
The man who has learned to yield now yields before the descent.
God spoke to Israel in the visions of the night, and said:
Jacob, Jacob.
He said: Here I am.
Jacob, Jacob.
The double name.
The same pattern as Abraham, Abraham at the Akedah.
The same pattern as Moses, Moses at the burning bush.
The double call marks a moment of divine urgency.
God speaks at the boundary, before the descent.
Here I am..
The third in the Jacob-Joseph narrative.
Abraham said it at the Akedah, before the descent to Moriah.
Joseph said it when his father sent him toward his brothers,
before the descent to the pit.
Now Jacob says it when God calls him,
before the descent to Egypt.
Three.at three descents.
The Cup of willingness,
poured at every descent The Jacob who fled from Esau did not stop to listen.
The Jacob who wrestled demanded a blessing.
Now: here I am.
No negotiation.
No demand.
No vow with conditions.
Just: presence.
The man who said if at Bethel now says here I am at Beersheba.
The conditional has become availability.
The vessel that set terms now holds still.
He said: I am God, the God of your father.
Do not be afraid to go down into Egypt,
for there I will make of you a great nation.
Do not fear.
The same command God gave to Isaac at Gerar: do not fear,
for I am with you.
The covenant's recurring command at moments of descent.
God speaks directly, I am God.
The same self-identification as Bethel: I am the Lord,
the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac.
The God who appeared in a dream at the beginning of Jacob's journey now speaks in a vision at the end of his time in Canaan.
Do not fear going down to Egypt.
The descent is named, and authorized.
God does not just allow the descent.
He commands it.
The same God who told Jacob to return to Canaan now tells him to leave for Egypt.
The covenant's geography shifts, by divine instruction.
The land that was promised is now the land they are leaving.
The promise does not depend on being in the land.
It depends on God being with the people.
I will make you a great nation there.
The covenant promise, renewed at the descent.
The same promise given to Abraham, to Isaac, to Jacob at Bethel.
Now: there.
In Egypt.
In the foreign land.
The covenant will grow in exile.
The Cup that was carried in the promised land will fill in the foreign land.
I will go down with you to Egypt.
And I will also surely bring you up again.
And Joseph's hand shall be on your eyes.
I will go down with you.
Not just I will be with you, I will go down.
God descends.
The covenant's God accompanies the covenant carrier into the foreign land.
The God who appeared at Bethel and said I will not leave you now says:
I will go down with you.
The God who went up from Jacob at Bethel now goes down with Jacob to Egypt.
I will bring you up again.
The return is promised before the descent begins.
The Cup of sojourning:
God accompanies both the going down and the coming up.
The descent is real.
The return is certain.
The four-hundred-year prophecy spoken to Abraham,
your offspring will be sojourners in a land not theirs, begins here.
But God already promises the end of the sojourning before it starts.
Joseph's hand shall be on your eyes.
The son thought dead will close the father's eyes at death.
The most intimate image in the chapter.
The son who was stripped, sold, imprisoned, elevated,
will place his hand on his father's eyes.
The son who was hidden for twenty-two years will be the one who closes the father's eyes.
The Cup of grief, held for twenty-two years,
deepened by a blood stained coat, confirmed by ten sons who lied,
is repaid with presence.
The false death answered by a real death,
attended by the living son.
Jacob rose up from Beersheba.
The sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, their little ones,
and their wives,
in the wagons which Pharaoh had sent to carry him.
The wagons.
The same wagons Jacob saw when his spirit revived.
The evidence that revived him now carries him.
The carts that proved Joseph was alive are now the carts that carry the father to Joseph.
The sons who once carried a blood-stained coat to Jacob now carry Jacob in Pharaoh's carts.
The Cup of the sons:
from carrying false evidence to carrying the father.
They took their livestock and their goods which they had acquired in the land of Canaan,
and came into Egypt, Jacob, and all his offspring with him.
His sons, and his sons' sons with him, his daughters,
and his sons' daughters.
He brought all his offspring with him into Egypt.
All his seed.
The covenant carrier brings everything.
No halfway.
No leaving some behind.
The Cup of the family, complete.
The entire household moves.
The land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is left,
by divine command.
The covenant does not depend on being in the land.
It depends on God being with the people.
Seventy souls enter Egypt.
Seventy.
The complete number.
Sixty-six who came with Jacob, plus Joseph, Manasseh,
and Ephraim already in Egypt, seventy.
The covenant family enters Egypt as seventy.
The number that will become as numerous as the stars of heaven.
The names are listed, every son, every grandson.
Not just the covenant carriers, all of them.
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, with Perez and Zerah, the breach,
the scandal's fruit.
The Cup of the scandal travels with the Cup of the family.
Joseph and Benjamin, the sons of Rachel.
Dan and Naphtali, the sons of Bilhah.
Gad and Asher, the sons of Zilpah.
All twelve.
All held.
The list includes Judah's sons: Er and Onan, dead in Canaan.
Shelah.
Perez and Zerah.
The breach, Perez, born through Tamar's boldness and Judah's confession,
is in the list.
The covenant goes into Egypt carrying the scandal's fruit.
The Cup that traveled through Judah's seal and Tamar's veil now travels in the genealogy of the seventy.
He sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph,
to show the way before him to Goshen.
They came to the land of Goshen.
Judah sent ahead.
to point, to guide, to direct.
Judah, the betrayer who became the substitute, is now the guide.
The one who went down from his brothers in chapter thirty-eight now goes ahead of his brothers.
The one who said sell him now leads the family to him.
The Cup of trust, given to the one who confessed, guaranteed,
and substituted.
Judah's arc: sell him, confess, guarantee, substitute, guide.
The betrayer has become the leader.
The covenant line, through Perez, through David, through Christ,
passes through a man whose journey from betrayal to guidance is the arc of the entire family.
Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen.
He presented himself to him.
He fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while.
The fourth weeping.
Joseph on Jacob's neck.
and he wept on his neck a good while.
The longest weeping yet.
Not the brief hidden tears of chapter forty-two.
Not the room tears of chapter forty-three.
Not the public loud weeping of chapter forty-five.
This weeping is prolonged.
A good while.
The weeping that was hidden, then brief, then loud, now extends.
The Cup of weeping: the longer the separation, the longer the tears.
Twenty-two years of grief pour out in a prolonged embrace.
The third neck-embrace.
The pattern completes.
Esau and Jacob, brothers reconciled.
Joseph and Benjamin, brothers reunited.
Joseph and Jacob, father and son reunited.
The neck embrace that began at the Jabbok,
when Esau ran to meet Jacob and fell on his neck,
now returns at Goshen.
The Cup that was held by a father who wept and refused comfort is now held by a son who weeps on the father's neck.
Israel said to Joseph: Now let me die,
since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.
Now let me die.
The father who said I shall go down to Sheol to my son,
mourning, now says: let me die.
Not in grief.
In fulfillment.
The Cup that held death for twenty-two years is now so full of life that the father can say:
I have seen enough.
The son I mourned is alive.
The eyes that wept over a blood-stained coat now see the living face.
Let me die, not because I am hopeless,
but because I am complete.
Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's house:
I will go up and speak with Pharaoh, and will tell him:
My brothers and my father's house,
who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
These men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock,
and they have brought their flocks, and their herds,
and all that they have.
It will happen, when Pharaoh summons you, and will say:
What is your occupation?
that you shall say:
Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now,
both we, and our fathers.
That you may dwell in the land of Goshen,
for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.
Goshen.
The land of separation.
Joseph instructs his brothers to tell Pharaoh they are shepherds,
because shepherds are an abomination to the Egyptians.
The covenant family will be set apart.
Not by their own choice, by Egyptian prejudice.
The Cup that entered Egypt as an honored family will be separated by the very culture that welcomed them.
The abomination that begins as cultural distance will become the seed of the enslavement that God prophesied to Abraham.
For every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.
The covenant family enters Egypt as shepherds,
the profession that makes them outsiders.
The same Cup that was carried by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,
all shepherds, now marks them as separate.
The land of Goshen will become the land of Israel's growth,
and then the land of Israel's bondage.
The descent that began as a family reunion will become a national enslavement.
The seventy who entered as honored guests will become the millions who cry out for deliverance.
But that is later.
For now, the father has seen the son.
The weeping has happened.
The Cup of the covenant has entered Egypt.
Seventy souls.
Carried by wagons.
Guided by Judah.
Met by Joseph.
Accompanied by God.
The God who said I will go down with you has gone down.
The God who said I will bring you up again has not yet brought them up.
But the promise stands.
The descent is real.
The return is certain.
And between the descent and the return,
between the entry into Goshen and the exodus from it,
the covenant will grow from seventy to a nation.
In the foreign land.
Under the foreign king.
In the land that receives shepherds as an abomination.
The Cup holds.
It has gone down.
It will come up.
